title: Cache-aside, write-through, write-back
summary: Who fills the cache, who updates it on a write, and what each choice risks.

blocks.p: A cache sits next to a database, and both hold the same data. Two questions follow. When a read misses, who loads the data into the cache? When the data changes, who updates the cache, and in what order?
The answers decide how fresh reads are, how fast writes are, and what you lose if the cache fails. There are three common answers.

The app talks to both. On a read, it checks the cache. On a miss, it reads the database and writes the result into the cache. On a write, it updates the database and then deletes the cached copy, so the next read loads the new value.

The cache only ever holds data someone asked for, and if it fails, reads fall back to the database. This is the most common strategy. Microsoft's guide describes it as the [cache-aside pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside).

blocks.caption: Cache-aside: a read that misses, a read that hits, and a write that deletes the cached copy.

blocks.p: Deleting is safer than updating the cached copy. If two writes race to update the cache, the older value can land last and stay there. A delete has no value to get wrong. The invalidation lesson covers the race that remains.

Every write goes to the cache and the database together, and the write finishes only when both have it. Reads after a write find fresh data in the cache. The cost is a slower write, and the cache fills with data that may never be read.

Also called write-behind. The write goes to the cache and finishes at once. The cache writes to the database later, often in batches. Writes are fast, and many writes to the same key become one database write.
The risk is loss. A write that is in the cache but not yet in the database is lost if the cache fails before it saves the write.

blocks.caption: Write-through waits for the database. Write-back returns at once and saves later. If the cache fails first, the write is gone.

list: **Cache-aside is the default.** Facebook's memcache paper calls it a demand-filled look-aside cache, and describes deleting keys on update rather than setting new values. See [Scaling Memcache at Facebook](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala).
**Read-through is cache-aside, moved.** Some caching libraries load from the database themselves on a miss, so the app only talks to the cache. The behaviour is the same.

**Write-back is everywhere below the app.** Operating systems and disk controllers hold writes in memory and save them later. Databases protect against the loss with a log written to disk before the write is acknowledged.

**AWS documents the trade-offs too.** The [ElastiCache caching strategies page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html) compares lazy loading, its name for cache-aside, with write-through.
Cache-aside: the app reads the cache, fills it on a miss, and deletes the key after a write.
Write-through: writes update cache and database together, so reads stay fresh but writes are slower.
Write-back: writes go to the cache and reach the database later, so writes are fast but can be lost.
Delete cached copies on write rather than updating them.
